title: Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation would turn an existing software system into a reviewable account of its behavior: modular contracts describing its components, interfaces, dependencies, and constraints, together with machine-checked evidence that the legacy implementation satisfies those contracts. It would explicitly identify the behavior and proof obligations left unresolved. The purpose is to make those recovered contracts useful enough to support verified repairs and replacements, including systems whose important behavior was never formally documented.

As a synthesis of the target capability, sound recovery means that accepted claims follow under stated programming-language semantics and environment assumptions. It does not require recovering every property of every program. A useful result must distinguish proved contracts, assumptions, and an explicit residual of unproved obligations. Recovering behavior also does not establish that the behavior is desirable: undocumented bugs and historical conventions may be part of what a replacement must preserve or deliberately change.

significance.text: Legacy modernization faces a concrete compatibility problem: enhancements or replacements can fail to compose safely with the surrounding system, while formal specifications needed for verified construction may be unavailable. Sound recovery at production scale could replace substantial manual reconstruction with human-auditable contracts and checkable conformance arguments. Its revolutionary contribution would be making verified component replacement practical for systems that were not originally developed around formal contracts.

The compatibility guarantee requires more than proving properties of the old code. The replacement must also satisfy the recovered contract, and that contract must constrain the observations that matter to callers and the surrounding system. Preserving selected invariants can establish preservation of those properties without establishing full behavioral equivalence. The Daikon and ESC/Java integration work describes checking modifications against previously inferred and checked specifications, providing a limited predecessor to this mechanism.

Conditional downstream possibilities include safer modernization of financial and safety-critical software, replacement of obsolete components, and more deliberate separation of required compatibility from behavior that should change. These are prospective consequences, not demonstrated sector-wide outcomes. Guarantees would remain conditional on the modeled language, dependencies, environment, and trusted verification components. Physical-system safety, fitness for intended use, and regulatory acceptance would require additional evidence; assumptions about the physical environment must be stated explicitly rather than hidden inside an unrestricted residual.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is a useful, sound, scalable integration of specification recovery and verification. It must infer modular contracts strong enough to verify designated replacements, establish that the legacy system satisfies them, and expose remaining obligations. DARPA's V-SPELLS goals identify central engineering challenges: recovering architecture and domain models, making interfaces and dependencies explicit, automating specification inference, and enabling developers to compose verified new components safely with existing code.

Execution-based inference alone cannot supply the guarantee. A property that holds in observed runs may fail on an untested execution, so inferred candidates require further justification. Combining dynamic inference with static checking is already a demonstrated idea; the unresolved integration challenge includes establishing the assumptions used by the checker and obtaining enough verified properties to support meaningful replacement. In the RV'01 prototype, some ownership annotations were introduced without source analysis and could be unsafe, illustrating how apparently helpful proof inputs can weaken an end-to-end assurance claim.

General limits on static inference also matter: the reviewed TSE material discusses true properties that cannot be computed and properties dependent on how a program is used, including its inputs. This supports bounded recovery under explicit assumptions, but it does not establish a precise impossibility theorem for an unspecified task called exact inference. The scientific problem must identify the property language, program class, and desired guarantees before a specific undecidability claim can be evaluated.

As an engineering synthesis, success must balance soundness, contract strength, modularity, and cost. A weak contract can be easy to prove yet inadequate for compatibility; an enormous residual can conceal almost all useful behavior. Conversely, contracts too detailed or expensive to understand and maintain may defeat the modernization purpose. The supplied historical evidence motivates these challenges but does not establish whether the full target capability remains unavailable as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The supplied DARPA V-SPELLS page marks the program complete and states that the page is no longer maintained. It describes a developer-accessible approach to incremental enhancement of legacy software, including inferred architecture and domain models, specification inference, and safe composition of verified components. Its resulting-tools section lists a demonstration of Taphos, Oxide, and Walrus. The reviewed page does not claim sound behavioral recovery of an entire production system; that absence on this page does not establish that no such result exists elsewhere.

Nimmer and Ernst's RV'01 preliminary paper reports combining Daikon's dynamic invariant inference with ESC/Java static checking on small programs. Dynamic inference proposes properties from executions, and the paper explicitly recognizes that these candidates need not hold over every possible execution. Subsequent static checking is a meaningful achievement beyond mining alone. However, the prototype's potentially unsafe ownership annotations prevent its reported checks from establishing the stronger end-to-end sound recovery envisaged here. This limitation narrows the result's guarantee without negating the reported experiments.

Ernst, Cockrell, Griswold, and Notkin reported accurate and useful invariant inference, at least for small programs, in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 27(2), pages 99–123, February 2001. The supplied review supports this scoped conclusion from the abstract and discusses inference limits from the associated paper. The abstract is a partial representation of the publication, and extraction of the retained full-paper text truncates on page 23; the relevant discussion of static-inference limits was available before that truncation. These materials support a dated, limited result rather than production-scale recovery.

The research also cites Lathouwers and Huisman's 2024 Survey of annotation generators for deductive verifiers and attributes to it a conclusion that generated specifications fall far short of a deductive-verification baseline. No captured text for this source was supplied, so that conclusion and the document's identity could not be assessed in the review. It remains an unverified attribution in this record, not an established finding or evidence that the survey is wrong.

The supplied record contains no freshness search with which to assess the frontier as of November 1, 2026. The historical experiments and completed-program description establish motivation and partial predecessors, but they establish neither achievement nor present-day absence of the proposed integrated capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: demonstrate the method on a production system of at least one million lines, or a smaller system with documented regulatory evidence that rewriting is prohibitively costly. Produce a human-reviewable modular specification, a machine-checked legacy conformance proof covering a predeclared substantial subset, and a clean-room reimplementation checked against the same recovered contract. The size threshold, regulatory alternative, and clean-room requirement are proposed evaluation choices, not published standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Million-line or regulatory-alternative conformance proof and clean-room replacement

completion_criteria.text: Before evaluation, define the observations that constitute compatibility, the language semantics, environment and dependency assumptions, trusted components, minimum contract coverage, and an acceptably bounded residual with explicit outstanding obligations. Explain why the recovered contracts are strong enough for the designated replacement task. Report environmental assumptions separately from unproved implementation behavior, so a successful proof cannot conceal its limits through an unconstrained residual.
completion_criteria.label: Assumptions separated from unproved behavior, bounded residual, replacement justification

completion_criteria.text: A proposed pre-registered differential suite should exercise declared interfaces and operating conditions, with any observed disagreements confined to the stated residual. Such testing would corroborate the proofs and help reveal modeling or integration mistakes; it cannot prove that every possible disagreement is confined to that residual. Evaluation across multiple systems would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested domains, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered differential suite confines disagreements to the stated residual

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, independent evaluators should be able to rerun the recovery process and proof checks from the evaluated code, configurations, assumptions, and tool versions. Report human annotation effort, recovery and checking costs, unresolved obligations, and the boundary of the trusted verification machinery. Developers who are not verification experts should then replace a subsystem using the recovered interfaces and verify the replacement against its contract. This proposed usability test would show whether the recovered knowledge supports practical maintenance rather than only an expert-led demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Independent rerun, full recovery accounting, and non-expert verified replacement

related_concepts.text: The following relationships are conceptual interpretations of the supplied roster titles, whose full definitions were not supplied. SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems, overlaps directly in legacy modernization. SWE-06 reconstructs useful contracts and checks legacy conformance; SWE-11 concerns preservation of behavior through transformation under defined semantics. Recovery can support transformation, but transformation can also rely on direct equivalence arguments or language semantics without a separately recovered specification. SWE-01, Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems, similarly concerns assurance across a compilation step rather than discovering a legacy system's modular contracts.

SWE-02, Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications, could consume recovered contracts to construct replacements, provided those contracts are adequate for the task. SWE-03, Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment, addresses a separate obligation: determining whether a specification captures what is wanted and the relevant operating world. SWE-06 establishes what legacy code satisfies under stated assumptions; that alone cannot establish intended correctness.

SWE-04, A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail, and SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries, concern reasoning about interacting components. Recovered contracts could supply inputs to such reasoning, while those concepts could help establish system-level consequences of component guarantees. SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change, concerns maintaining assurance as software evolves; recovered interfaces and obligations could provide a starting point, but efficient ongoing assurance is a distinct capability.

SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs, could help enforce boundaries around a component with incompletely recovered behavior, but confinement would not explain that behavior or prove replacement compatibility. SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution, and SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code, concern particular execution guarantees that recovery might seek to characterize. Establishing either guarantee would not by itself recover the wider contract of a legacy system.

unresolved_issues: Whether the integrated capability has been demonstrated at useful production scale as of November 1, 2026 remains unassessed because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The cited 2024 survey's identity, scope, and attributed conclusion remain unverified because no captured text was supplied.
A precise inference problem is needed before attaching a specific undecidability result to the target capability.
The proposed evaluation still requires operational definitions of substantial coverage, sufficient contract strength, acceptable residual size, and practical cost.
Full definitions of the related roster concepts were not supplied; their relationships are interpretations of titles, particularly the candidate-specific scope of SWE-11.
The associated 2001 TSE paper's retained extraction is truncated, limiting conclusions about material beyond the passages covered by the supplied review.

brief.title: Recovering the rules old software lives by
possible: When old software needs replacing, developers could recover the rules its parts follow, even when nobody wrote them down. These contracts—precise descriptions of behavior and dependencies—would come with computer-checked proofs that the old code follows them, plus a clear account of what remains unproved.

Developers could then check a replacement against the same contracts before putting it into service. This would let them preserve behavior that other software relies on and deliberately choose what should change.
why: Replacing one part of a large software system can break the parts around it. Recovering usable contracts could reduce the manual work of reconstructing those connections and make verified replacement practical for software built without formal specifications.
Teams maintaining financial or safety-critical software could use this capability to replace obsolete components and modernize systems piece by piece.

sources.showed: This is a survey of tools that generate annotations, the statements supplied to software proof checkers.
sources.cited_for: It concerns automatic generation of statements used in software proofs.
sources.not_established: A survey does not itself demonstrate recovery and verified replacement of a production system.

sources.showed: The completed V-SPELLS program pursued tools for recovering software structure and safely combining replacement components with existing code. It lists a demonstration of resulting tools.
sources.cited_for: The program identifies the engineering challenges of recovering contracts and safely replacing components.
sources.not_established: The program description does not demonstrate sound recovery of an entire production system's behavior.

sources.who: Jeremy W. Nimmer and Michael D. Ernst
sources.showed: Their preliminary prototype inferred rules from test runs, then checked them by reasoning about code. On small programs, the checker accepted all or most proposed rules.
sources.quote:
In preliminary experiments, ESC/Java veriﬁed all or
most of the invariants proposed by Daikon.
sources.cited_for: Automatic discovery of behavioral rules can be combined with checking them against code.
sources.not_established: Potentially unsafe assumptions about data ownership prevent an end-to-end guarantee.

sources.who: Michael D. Ernst, Jake Cockrell, William G. Griswold, and David Notkin
sources.showed: Daikon recovered behavioral rules from program runs. On small programs, it rediscovered known rules and found others that helped developers modify code.
sources.quote:
These
experiments demonstrate that, at least for small programs, invariant
inference is both accurate and useful.
sources.cited_for: Rules inferred from executions can help programmers understand and change small programs.
sources.not_established: Rules observed in test runs need not hold on every execution, and usefulness on small programs does not establish production-scale recovery.

shown: Nimmer and Ernst demonstrated an automatic pipeline that discovers behavioral rules from executions and checks them against code. Their preliminary experiments worked on small programs, but potentially unsafe assumptions about which code controls data limited the guarantee.

Ernst and colleagues also showed that inferred rules could help with software modification on small programs. DARPA's completed V-SPELLS program pursued the broader goal of recovering software structure and supporting compatible replacements.
missing: A production-scale demonstration must combine useful recovered contracts, checked proofs about the old code, and a replacement checked against those contracts.
The assumptions used in proofs must be justified, with unproved behavior listed separately and kept within meaningful bounds.
Recovered contracts must capture enough behavior to justify replacement while remaining understandable and affordable to maintain.
Independent teams and developers without verification expertise must be able to repeat the process and use its results.

milestones.label: Large-system proof and independently written replacement
milestones.explanation: A million-line system, or a smaller one with documented regulatory barriers to rewriting, would need reviewable contracts, a substantial checked proof and an independently written replacement. Both would have to satisfy the same contracts.

milestones.label: Explicit assumptions and bounded unproved behavior
milestones.explanation: Evaluation would define compatibility, language rules, environment assumptions, trusted tools, minimum coverage and bounded unproved behavior separately. This would establish whether the contracts justify the intended replacement.

milestones.label: Predetermined comparisons find only declared differences
milestones.explanation: Tests fixed in advance would compare old and replacement code across declared interfaces and conditions, with differences confined to declared unproved behavior. This would corroborate proofs and expose modeling mistakes.

milestones.label: Independent repetition and replacement by ordinary developers
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluators would repeat recovery and proof checks, accounting for human work, costs, unresolved claims and trusted tools. Developers without verification expertise would then verify a subsystem replacement to test practical use.

uncertain: How much behavior must contracts cover, and how little may remain unproved, for a replacement guarantee to be useful?
Can recovery produce contracts strong enough for compatibility at a practical cost across different kinds of systems?
Comparison tests can reveal disagreements but cannot establish that every possible disagreement falls within the declared unproved behavior.

page.title: Specification inference for verified legacy modernization
page.definition: Recover modular contracts from legacy source code. Each contract states what callers must supply and what behavior the component guarantees in return. Machine-checked proofs establish that the original component satisfies the contract and that a replacement preserves the specified behavior on which callers rely.

goal.need: A U.S. tax system that issues notices and reports refund status had 75,000 reported users in 2025. Its business rules are embedded in aging code that fewer specialists can maintain. Even a replacement built exactly to its documentation can break callers if the documentation misses behavior they rely on. Recovering those dependencies would let maintainers upgrade one component for security or speed while preserving the services that use it. They still need to distinguish required behavior from defects in the old code.

figures.caption: Coverage of verification annotations in the 2024 comparison
figures.note: The three examples were a counter, binary search and an arraylist. These percentages count baseline annotations; they do not measure the fraction of program behavior proved.

statements.quote: Provably safe composition of enhancements with the rest of the system.
statements.context: The solicitation lists this challenge alongside specification inference and recovery of domain models from legacy code.

completion.title: Recovered contracts justify a verified legacy replacement at V-SPELLS’s final code scale.
completion.criterion: Machine-check legacy conformance to recovered modular contracts and replacement conformance to the same contracts, and prove that these contracts imply preservation of the stated interface observations. State the language semantics, environmental assumptions and trusted dependencies. Discharge every proof obligation needed for that compatibility claim; identify other unproved behavior separately. Demonstrate the conjunction at V-SPELLS’s final scale of 1000Ks source lines.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis using DARPA’s final code-scale target and the static-verification criterion.
completion.basis: Searched V-SPELLS’s solicitation and completion page, the 2024 annotation-generator survey, and contract-inference papers for an acceptance test combining legacy conformance, contract sufficiency and verified replacement. No such integrated test was found. This synthesis retains V-SPELLS’s published final code scale and the field’s static-verification criterion.

milestones.title: Recovered candidate invariants survive every observed run of a program’s test suite.
milestones.criterion: Infer candidate preconditions, postconditions and loop invariants from execution traces. Report a candidate only if no observation falsifies it and enough observations support it under the detector’s plausibility test.
milestones.set_by: Dynamic invariant-detection convention described by Ernst and colleagues, Sections 2 and 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: those invariants that are tested to a sufficient degree without falsification are reported to the programmer.

milestones.title: A static verifier establishes inferred contracts under its stated assumptions.
milestones.criterion: Submit inferred contracts and the implementation to a static verifier. Count a contract as established only if the verifier discharges the obligations for that contract under its stated assumptions.
milestones.set_by: Static-verification convention described by Nimmer and Ernst, Section 1, and applied in the Move Prover inference workflow.
milestones.threshold_quote: A static verifier can indicate which proposed invariants are guaranteed to be true.

milestones.title: Legacy-code understanding reaches at least 60% accuracy and over 70% code coverage.
milestones.criterion: At a scale of tens of thousands of source lines, instrument all accesses to domain data types and all operations on them. Achieve at least 60% program-understanding accuracy and more than 70% code coverage.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, V-SPELLS solicitation, Table 1, Phase 1 indicative target.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least 60% accuracy with over 70% code coverage

milestones.title: Legacy-code composition reaches 80% program-understanding accuracy and 90% coverage.
milestones.criterion: At a scale of hundreds of thousands of source lines, make all domain operations programmable in a domain-specific language while maintaining compatibility with native code. Achieve 80% program-understanding accuracy and 90% coverage.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, V-SPELLS solicitation, Table 1, Phase 2 indicative target.

milestones.title: At million-line scale, program understanding reaches 95% accuracy and 99.9% coverage.
milestones.criterion: At a scale of millions of source lines, translate all code to a domain-specific language or virtual machine except for a few enclaves that can be analyzed effectively. Achieve 95% program-understanding accuracy and 99.9% coverage.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, V-SPELLS solicitation, Table 1, Phase 3 indicative target.

milestones.title: An inferred component contract suffices to verify a caller’s stated property.
milestones.criterion: Verify the caller using the inferred contract in place of the called implementation. At the call, prove the component’s preconditions. Use its guaranteed postconditions to discharge the caller’s proof obligation.
milestones.set_by: Modular verification convention documented in the OpenJML method-call tutorial.
milestones.threshold_quote: we replace the call of `callee()` in the caller’s body with the callee’s pre- and post-conditions.

milestones.title: A compatible driver replaces a problematic driver in a large monolithic system.
milestones.criterion: In the V-SPELLS Phase 1 example, replace a known problematic driver with a correct, compatible version written in a domain-specific language. Use a subsystem that lacks instrumentation like that provided by the Berkeley Packet Filter and add that instrumentation to the subsystem.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, V-SPELLS solicitation, Exemplary Evaluation, Phase 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: with a correct and compatible DSL version

milestones.title: A component is replaced in a large distributed legacy system.
milestones.criterion: Use the modernization tools to replace a component within a large distributed legacy system. Demonstrate the replacement in the context of the surrounding system.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, V-SPELLS Phase 2 exemplary evaluation and FY 2023 programme plan.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate utility by replacing a component in a large legacy distributed system.

not_found: No published acceptance test was found for the integrated completion criterion.
No operational definitions of V-SPELLS’s accuracy and coverage percentages were found in its public solicitation.
Searches for V-SPELLS evaluations and final reports found no public result establishing attainment of its Phase 1, 2 or 3 recovery targets.
No programme, standards-body or professional-society statement disputing the feasibility or value of verified legacy component replacement was found.

results.detail: Two DisjSets candidates produced warnings and 62 could not be expressed in ESCJML. The ownership annotations were added heuristically without source analysis.
results.quote:
ESC proved 80 of the 82 expressible invariants, and it warned
about two (unprovable) test suite artifacts.

results.finding: ESC/Java verified 530 of 554 evaluated Daikon clauses across 11 Java programs.
results.detail: ESC/Java omits arithmetic overflow and alias tracking, models zero or one loop iterations, and allows unchecked assumptions.

results.finding: ESC/Java verified its runtime safety checks for all 8 methods of StackAr using generated specifications.

successfully

results.finding: AutoSpec verified stated properties for 199 of 251 C benchmark programs using inferred specifications.
results.detail: The benchmark count measures successful program-level proofs. It does not count all individual contracts established, since some unsuccessful programs also had validated annotations.
results.quote:
The result shows AutoSpec can successfully handle
79% (= 199 / 251) programs with various structures

results.finding: AutoSpec verified the caller’s property in the pointer-sum benchmark in 5 of 5 runs using the inferred add contract.
results.detail: The paper reports the successful modular proof and shows the inferred callee contract. It does not print the individual call-site verification conditions.
results.quote:
The subsequently generated specification (line 4) states
the add function has no assignment behavior, making the verification succeed.

results.finding: Java PathFinder-guided Path2Spec achieved a 42.3% static verification pass rate across 385 Java programs.
results.detail: The reported rate measures downstream static verification. Java PathFinder produced usable paths for 81 of the 385 programs.
results.quote: using path information extracted by JPF as guidance to generate formal specifications achieves an overall %Passed of 42.3%

results.finding: GPT-5 Path2Spec achieved an 84.4% OpenJML verification pass rate across 385 Java programs.
results.detail: OpenJML build 21-0-14 used a 30-minute timeout. Timeouts, detected violations, and other errors counted as failures.

Path2Spec
produces far more correct specifications than the state-of-the-art SpecGen
across all base models and benchmarks, reaching a best overall success rate of 84.4%

Notably, the 1,009 new counterexample test cases

results.finding: ABDUCTOR established consistent heap contracts for all 121 procedures in the modified Windows IEEE 1394 driver.
results.detail: The analysis ignored concurrency and modeled unknown library calls and calls through function pointers as nondeterministic assignments without side effects.
results.quote:
Our analysis was able to ﬁnd consistent speciﬁcations (where
precondition is not inconsistent) for all 121 of the procedures.

results.finding: In the 121-procedure Windows IEEE 1394 driver, inferred callee contracts supported proofs of higher-level procedures’ Hoare triples.
results.detail: The stated caller properties are the preconditions and postconditions in the resulting Hoare triples. The experiment used a slightly modified driver.
results.quote:
our analysis has found proofs of
the Hoare triples for higher-level procedures, which would have
been impossible if the specs discovered for sub-procedures were
too imprecise for the relevant call sites.

results.finding: On 50 C programs, 62% of SpecAgent synthesis trajectories passed the Frama-C/WP verification gate by six invocations.

definition = "Recover modular contracts from legacy source code. Each contract states what callers must supply and what behavior the component guarantees in return. Machine-checked proofs establish that the original component satisfies the contract and that a replacement preserves the specified behavior on which callers rely.". Reason: The definition now explains what a caller must supply and what a replacement must preserve.

goal.need = "A U.S. tax system that issues notices and reports refund status had 75,000 reported users in 2025. Its business rules are embedded in aging code that fewer specialists can maintain. Even a replacement built exactly to its documentation can break callers if the documentation misses behavior they rely on. Recovering those dependencies would let maintainers upgrade one component for security or speed while preserving the services that use it. They still need to distinguish required behavior from defects in the old code.". Reason: The Java benchmark measures annotation recovery, while the tax-system example shows who depends on legacy software and why a compatible replacement matters.
